Despite\\nbeing accessible from the Internet, the endpoint is still considered\\nsecure because it requires all API requests to be authenticated by IAM\\nand then authorized by Kubernetes RBAC. That said, if your corporate\\nsecurity policy mandates that you restrict access to the API from the\\nInternet or prevents you from routing traffic outside the cluster VPC,\\nyou can:\\n\\n* Configure the EKS cluster endpoint to be private. See\\n Modifying\\n Cluster Endpoint Access for further information on this topic.\\n* Leave the cluster endpoint public and specify which CIDR blocks can\\n communicate with the cluster endpoint. The blocks are effectively a\\n whitelisted set of public IP addresses that are allowed to access the\\n cluster endpoint.\\n* Configure public access with a set of whitelisted CIDR blocks and set\\n private endpoint access to enabled. This will allow public access from a\\n specific range of public IPs while forcing all network traffic between\\n the kubelets (workers) and the Kubernetes API through the cross-account\\n ENIs that get provisioned into the cluster VPC when the control plane is\\n provisioned\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eks/latest/best-practices/identity-and-access-management.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Introducing The CIS Amazon EKS Benchmark | Containers\",\"context\":\"## Containers\\n\\n# Introducing The CIS Amazon EKS Benchmark\\n\\nToday, we\u2019re announcing a new Center for Internet Security (CIS) benchmark for Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS). This new benchmark is optimized to help you accurately assess the security configuration of Amazon EKS clusters, including security assessments for nodes to help meet security and compliance requirements.\\n\\nSecurity is a critical consideration when configuring and maintaining Kubernetes clusters and applications. Amazon EKS provides secure, managed Kubernetes clusters by default, but you still need to ensure that you configure the nodes and applications securely and meet your security and compliance requirements. The CIS Kubernetes Benchmark provides good practice guidance on security configurations for unmanaged Kubernetes clusters where you typically manage the Kubernetes cluster control plane and nodes. The benchmark does not sufficiently cover the different configuration mechanisms used by Amazon EKS. This means that if you\u2019re using the CIS Kubernetes benchmark with EKS clusters you\u2019re faced with false positive errors. These errors incorrectly assert your clusters are not secure or properly configured. With the CIS Amazon EKS Benchmark, you now have guidance aligned to the Amazon EKS cluster configuration and you should use this benchmark to assess and configure security for your cluster nodes. You may use the recently published Amazon EKS Best Practices Guide for Security in conjunction with the CIS Amazon EKS Benchmark that we announce today.\\n\\nThe latest version of CIS Kubernetes Benchmark v1.5.1 provides guidance on security configurations for Kubernetes versions v1.15 for unmanaged Kubernetes clusters. The CIS Kubernetes Benchmark is scoped for implementations managing both the control plane, which includes `etcd`, API server, controller and scheduler, and the data plane, which is made up of one or more nodes. As Amazon EKS provides a fully managed control plane, not all of the recommendations from the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark are applicable as you are not responsible for configuring or managing the control plane. To ensure this scope is reflected with implementation specifics of Amazon EKS, we created the CIS Amazon EKS Benchmark starting from the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark and with the input of the community around specific configuration considerations for EKS clusters\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/containers/introducing-cis-amazon-eks-benchmark/\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) controls\",\"context\":\"## [CT.EKS.PR.1] Require an Amazon EKS cluster to be configured with public access disabled to the cluster Kubernetes API server endpoint\\n\\nThis control checks whether an Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) cluster endpoint disallows public access to the cluster Kubernetes API server endpoint.\\n\\n* **Control objective:** Limit network access\\n* **Implementation:** CloudFormation guard rule\\n* **Control behavior:** Proactive\\n* **Resource types:** `AWS::EKS::Cluster`\\n* **CloudFormation guard rule:**\\n CT.EKS.PR.1 rule specification\\n\\n**Details and examples**\\n\\n* For details about the PASS, FAIL, and SKIP behaviors associated with\\n this control, see the:\\n CT.EKS.PR.1 rule specification\\n* For examples of PASS and FAIL CloudFormation templates related to\\n this control, see:\\n CT.EKS.PR.1 example templates\\n\\n**Explanation**\\n\\nWhen you create a new cluster, Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) creates an endpoint for the managed Kubernetes API server, which you can use to communicate with your cluster using Kubernetes management tools, such as `kubectl`. By default, this API server endpoint is public to the internet, and access to the API server is secured using a combination of AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) along with native Kubernetes Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). Enabling private access to the Kubernetes API server ensures that all communication between your nodes and the API server stays within your VPC. {"id": "0dbe62a1-20d8-403d-bd33-fa1ab0538126", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "I checked all five controls against the live cluster. Four fail and one cannot be determined. The CIS v1.8.0 titles and audit criteria below come from my memory of the benchmark, not from documentation. `verify_aws_claim` returned only general AWS pages (the CIS blog, the EKS best-practices guide and a Control Tower control). None of them gave the v1.8.0 control text, so please confirm the titles against the CIS PDF.

Your expectations for all five controls match my recollection. The only difference is that 2.1.1 and 5.3.1 are manual-type recommendations in CIS, and the API evidence below still decides them.

**Cluster facts:** `cis-skill-test` in us-east-1 is ACTIVE on Kubernetes 1.37, platform version eks.9, in vpc-00000000000000001. It has one managed node group (`Nodegroup-EXAMPLE`, 2 × t3.medium, AL2023) and no Fargate profiles.

| Control | Status |
|---|---|
| 2.1.1 Enable audit logs | FAIL |
| 5.3.1 Encrypt Kubernetes Secrets with KMS CMKs | FAIL (see caveat) |
| 5.4.1 Restrict access to the control plane endpoint | FAIL |
| 5.4.2 Private endpoint enabled and public access disabled | FAIL |
| 5.4.3 Clusters are created with private nodes | FAIL |

**2.1.1 – Enable audit logs: FAIL**
- `logging.clusterLogging` has only `["api"]` enabled.
- `audit`, `authenticator`, `controllerManager` and `scheduler` are all `enabled: false`.
- Remediation: run `aws eks update-cluster-config --name cis-skill-test --logging '{"clusterLogging":[{"types":["api","audit","authenticator","controllerManager","scheduler"],"enabled":true}]}'`.

**5.3.1 – Encrypt Kubernetes Secrets with KMS CMKs: FAIL**
- The `describe_cluster` response has no `encryptionConfig` field, so no CMK is associated with the `secrets` resource.
- Caveat: EKS may encrypt secrets at rest by default with AWS-owned keys on recent versions. That doesn't meet this control, which requires a customer-managed KMS key.
- I made no KMS calls because there is no key ARN to check.
- Remediation: create a symmetric CMK with rotation enabled, then run `aws eks associate-encryption-config` with `resources:["secrets"]` and `provider.keyArn`. This is irreversible.

**5.4.1 – Restrict access to the control plane endpoint: FAIL**
- `endpointPublicAccess` is `true`.
- `publicAccessCidrs` is `["0.0.0.0/0"]`, so the API server is open to the whole internet.
- Remediation: set `publicAccessCidrs` to specific trusted CIDRs, or disable public access.

**5.4.2 – Private endpoint enabled and public access disabled: FAIL**
- `endpointPrivateAccess` is `true`, which is correct.
- `endpointPublicAccess` is `true`, which fails the control.
- Remediation: run `aws eks update-cluster-config --name cis-skill-test --resources-vpc-config endpointPublicAccess=false,endpointPrivateAccess=true`.

**5.4.3 – Clusters are created with private nodes: FAIL**
- Subnets: both subnets, `subnet-00000000000000001` (us-east-1a, 10.42.0.0/20) and `subnet-00000000000000002` (us-east-1b, 10.42.16.0/20), are used by the cluster and the node group. Both have `MapPublicIpOnLaunch: true`.
- Routing: both subnets are associated with route table `rtb-00000000000000001`. It has `0.0.0.0/0 → igw-00000000000000001` (active), so they are public subnets. There is no NAT gateway in the VPC.
- Instances: both running nodes have public IPs.

  | Instance | Subnet | Public IP |
  |---|---|---|
  | `i-1234567890abcdef0_1` | `subnet-00000000000000002` | 198.51.100.10 |
  | `i-1234567890abcdef0_2` | `subnet-00000000000000001` | 198.51.100.20 |

- Remediation: create private subnets with no IGW route (NAT gateway or VPC endpoints for egress) and `MapPublicIpOnLaunch=false`. Then replace the node group in those subnets. A node group's subnets can't be changed in place.

**Calls made:** All calls succeeded and none were denied. They were EKS `describe_cluster`, `list_nodegroups`, `list_fargate_profiles` and `describe_nodegroup`, plus EC2 `describe_subnets`, `describe_route_tables` and `describe_instances`. I did not call `kms:*`, `describe_security_groups` or CloudTrail, and I made no changes.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
